title: Kubeconfig & Multi-Cluster Contexts
intro: Most real setups juggle more than one cluster — local, staging, prod. This is how you point kubectl at the right one without cross-wiring them by accident.

steps.prompt: See every context, cluster, and user defined in your kubeconfig.
steps.fake_output:
apiVersion: v1
contexts:
- name: staging
  context: {cluster: staging-cluster, user: staging-user}
- name: prod
  context: {cluster: prod-cluster, user: prod-user}
current-context: staging
steps.explanation: A context is just a named (cluster, user, namespace) triple — this is the full picture of every cluster kubectl currently knows how to reach.
steps.why: 'kubectl config get-contexts' shows a friendlier table of just the names — 'config view' is what you'd use when you need the full detail, like which user/cert is tied to which cluster.

steps.prompt: List just the context names in table form.
steps.fake_output:
CURRENT   NAME      CLUSTER          AUTHINFO       NAMESPACE
*         staging   staging-cluster  staging-user
          prod      prod-cluster     prod-user
steps.explanation: The * marks which context is currently active — that's the cluster every kubectl command right now is actually hitting.
steps.why: This is the fast way to sanity-check 'wait, am I about to run this against prod?' before typing a destructive command — always worth a glance first.

steps.explanation: Every kubectl command after this now targets the prod cluster — this is exactly the kind of command you want to double- and triple-check before running.
steps.why: There's no kubectl-native confirmation prompt for this — many teams alias or color-code their shell prompt to show the active context specifically to prevent this kind of prod mistake.

steps.prompt: You're done in prod — switch back to 'staging'.
steps.explanation: Same command as before, just pointed the other way — always worth confirming with 'get-contexts' or 'current-context' after switching, not just trusting muscle memory.
steps.why: Getting in the habit of checking current-context after every switch is cheap insurance against the single most common multi-cluster mistake: running a command against the wrong cluster.
